brief.goal: Prepare five source choices about cockroaches, each teaching a different useful, less-obvious homeowner lesson with checked evidence.
brief.output: Five original source links with one- or two-sentence lesson previews (maximum four sentences/600 characters), plus internal publisher/date/species/region/limits, one to four factual statements and short exact evidence (at most 25 quoted words total per publication). Return fewer with a stated shortage if necessary. No hooks or scripts.
questions: Which five distinct original publications can support useful lessons about cockroach biology, behavior, identification or nonchemical prevention?
What does each source teach, why would a homeowner care, and does the main source itself support an honest hook?
Which exact passages support each lesson, and what species, geographic, date or evidence limits matter?
Are any candidates duplicate, reserved, inaccessible, too shallow or unsupported? What remains unknown?
scope_constraints: Audience: homeowners around New Braunfels and Central Texas. Research pest: cockroaches; do not default back to ants.
Prioritize useful, less-obvious explanations over generic tips. Explain what happens, why it happens and what a homeowner can understand or do.
Keep five choices varied by lesson and publication. No invented facts, quotes, dates, access, local measurements or viewer-performance claims.
Use only current verified public read/search capabilities. No paid fallback, model calls, cookie access, downloads to execute, or new logins.
Current acceptance domains: citybugs.tamu.edu, fireant.tamu.edu, extensionentomology.tamu.edu, agrilifeextension.tamu.edu, npic.orst.edu, epa.gov
Identification, behavior and nonchemical prevention only; no dosing, mixing, medical advice or product-specific directions.
A main source must support its hook promise. Supporting science is a separate request after hook selection.
No videos watched or authenticated social content accessed unless actual capability and retrieval are verified. Never substitute snippets for evidence.

Turkestan cockroaches are known to infest a variety of habitats such as semi-arid deserts, water meter boxes, compost piles, leaf litter, potted plants, sewer systems, and cracks in concrete walkways (See Texas Invasives webpage below).
Origin and Characteristics
The Turkestan cockroach, scientifically known as Blatta lateralis , also known as the rusty red cockroach or red runner cockroach, is native to an area extending from northern Africa to Central Asia.
Adult males, often confused for American cockroaches ( Periplaneta americana), are brownish orange/red, slender, and have long, yellowish wings which allow them to attract females and to glide. Compared to adult American cockroaches, adult male Turkestan cockroaches are smaller in size and, in my opinion, lighter in color.
